To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) uncertainty quantification in prognostics needs to be approached from a Bayesian perspective, (ii) uncertainty in prognostic parameters should be propagated through the remaining useful life model, (iii) uncertainty quantification is a challenging problem, and (iv) uncertainty in prognos-tic parameters can be propagated through the model using the Monte-Carlo simulation method.

uncertainty in prognostic and health management is best quantified using Bayesian methods, which can be used for uncertainty propagation to compute the overall uncertainty of the prognostic estimates.

(1) the subjective Bayesian approach to uncertainty is more suitable than the classical frequentist approach for uncertainty analysis in condition based prognostic and health monitoring applications, (2) uncertainty quantification in prognostics needs to be approached from the perspective of uncertainty propagation, and (3) there are several practical challenges in the uncertainty propagation based quantification of uncertainty, and the development of new methods and tools for this purpose is an active area of research.
In summary, our research is concerned with

the development and application of methods and algorithms for the prediction of the remaining useful life, with a focus on quantifying and interpreting the uncertainty associated with such predictions.
understanding and quantifying uncertainty in remaining useful life predictions, and developing methods to facilitate decision making under such uncertainty.
developing the theory and practice of uncertainty quantification in condition-based prognostics and life prediction.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
uncertainty quantification is a critical aspect in prognostics that needs to be addressed in the context of a specific prognostics application.
prognostics and uncertainty quantification are inseparable, and uncertainty quantification is a key enabler for meaningful prognostics-based decision making.
the uncertainty in remaining useful life predictions needs to be quantified, and this quantification needs to be based on a Bayesian approach to uncertainty.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Bayesian approach to prognostics is more suitable, and that uncertainty propagation methods can be used for computing the overall uncertainty in remaining useful life.

the uncertainty in remaining useful life predictions can be quantified by using a Bayesian approach to uncertainty quantification and propagating the uncertainty through the system model and the degradation process model, and that the uncertainty propagation methods that are currently available are not sufficient to address the challenges involved.

the Bayesian framework provides a more natural interpretation of uncertainty for condition based prognosics and health monitoring, while the frequentist approach can be used as an alternative for uncertainty quantification in such problems.
The main takeaway from our work is that
uncertainty quantification is an integral part of condition based prognostic decision making.
the Bayesian interpretation and quantification of the uncertainty associated with prognostics can be used to make better decisions, and to quantify the overall uncertainty in prognostic predictions.

the uncertainty in prognostic models can be quantified in a principled manner, and that this quantification can be useful in making decisions regarding maintenance and operation of systems and components.
